claim: The master gene trachealess is dispensable for the initiation of invagination.
source: The master gene trachealess is dispensable for the initiation of invagination, while it is essential for maintaining the invaginated structure, suggesting that tracheal morphogenesis and differentiation are separately induced.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data showing that trh mutants can initiate invagination (Figure 1B,C), and by the observation that di-phosphorylated ERK is detected in trh mutants at stage 10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: trachealess is essential for maintaining the invaginated structure.
source: The master gene trachealess is dispensable for the initiation of invagination, while it is essential for maintaining the invaginated structure, suggesting that tracheal morphogenesis and differentiation are separately induced.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging showing that trh mutants form transient invaginations that return to the surface (Figure 1C), and by fixed samples showing invaginated structures at stage 12 that disappear by stage 15-16 (Figure 1E-G).

claim: trachealess expression starts in bipotential tracheal/epidermal placode cells.
source: trachealess expression starts in bipotential tracheal/epidermal placode cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that initial Trh+ cells can become either tracheal or epidermal cells (Figure 2), with some cells losing Trh expression and remaining in the epidermis.

claim: After invagination, trachealess expression is maintained in the invaginated cells but is extinguished in the remaining sheet cells.
source: After invagination, its expression is maintained in the invaginated cells but is extinguished in the remaining sheet cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing experiments using R14E10-GAL4 driving nls-lacZ, showing trh-off cells in the epidermis and trh-on cells in invaginated tubules (Figure 2C-E, G).

claim: A trachealess cis-regulatory module (R15F01) shows both tracheal enhancer activity and silencer activity in the surface epidermal sheet.
source: A trachealess cis-regulatory module that shows both tracheal enhancer activity and silencer activity in the surface epidermal sheet was identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter assays showing R15F01 drives expression in tracheal cells but not epidermis (Figure 3B', G), and by domain mapping showing both enhancer and silencer elements (Figure 4, Figure 5).

claim: The coupling of trachealess expression with the invaginated structure ensures that only invaginated cells canalize robustly into the tracheal fate.
source: We propose that the coupling of trachealess expression with the invaginated structure ensures that only invaginated cells canalize robustly into the tracheal fate.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observation that Trh expression is maintained only in invaginated cells and that R15F01 activity is restricted to invaginated cells independent of invagination depth.

claim: Ten pairs of tracheal placodes form in the dorsal anterior part of the epidermis in each segment by stage 10.
source: Tracheal morphogenesis is initiated by placode specification; ten pairs of tracheal placodes form in the dorsal anterior part of the epidermis in each segment by stage 10, followed by invagination, branching and fusion (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of known tracheal development supported by the schematic in Figure 1A.

claim: trachealess is considered to be a master regulator of tracheal morphogenesis.
source: In this process, the tracheal placodes first appear as a group of cells expressing trachealess (trh), which is considered to be a master regulator of tracheal morphogenesis (Chung et al., 2011; Isaac and Andrew, 1996; Wilk et al., 1996), and then EGF signaling and mitosis synergistically drive invagination by generating centripetal pressure and inducing epithelial sheet buckling, respectively (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013; Nishimura et al., 2007; Ogura et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EGF signaling and mitosis synergistically drive invagination by generating centripetal pressure and inducing epithelial sheet buckling, respectively.
source: In this process, the tracheal placodes first appear as a group of cells expressing trachealess (trh), which is considered to be a master regulator of tracheal morphogenesis (Chung et al., 2011; Isaac and Andrew, 1996; Wilk et al., 1996), and then EGF signaling and mitosis synergistically drive invagination by generating centripetal pressure and inducing epithelial sheet buckling, respectively (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013; Nishimura et al., 2007; Ogura et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FGF signaling triggers tracheal branching.
source: Finally, FGF signaling triggers tracheal branching (Figure 1A) (Glazer and Shilo, 1991; Sutherland et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In trh mutants, apical constriction forming a tracheal pit appears in the center of the placode region, followed by mitosis in the pit cells and rapid, deep invagination.
source: Live imaging of trh1 (an EMS-induced missense allele) mutants at single-cell resolution revealed an unexpected finding: apical constriction forming a tracheal pit appeared in the center of the placode region, followed by mitosis in the pit cells and rapid, deep invagination as seen in the control, although the onset of invagination was delayed (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: In trh mutants, the invaginated structure gradually returns to the surface epidermal layer and merges with these cells to form a segmental furrow.
source: Over the next 90 min, the invaginated structure gradually returned to the surface epidermal layer and merged with these cells to form a segmental furrow, leaving no trace of the tracheal structure (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In trhA14-3/trhB16-11 mutants, would-be tracheal placode cells form a tracheal pit and invaginated structures during stages 11–13.
source: Consistent with this live imaging analysis of trh1, in fixed samples with a heteroallelic combination of TALEN-induced trh null alleles (trhA14-3/trhB16-11, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Kondo et al., 2014), would-be tracheal placode cells labeled with the R14E10 trh primary enhancer (containing the trh66 STAT-responsive element that mediates stage-10 trh expression in the placode (Sotillos et al., 2010), Figure 1D) also formed a tracheal pit (Figure 1E) and formed invaginated structures during stages 11–13 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by fixed sample imaging data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: In trhA14-3/trhB16-11 mutants, R14E10-positive cells return to the surface epidermal layer at stage 15.
source: These R14E10-positive cells returned to the surface epidermal layer at stage 15 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by fixed sample imaging data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The appearance of invaginated structures at stage 12 and the disappearance of these structures at stages 15–16 were observed with 100% penetrance.
source: The appearance of invaginated structures at stage 12 and the disappearance of these structures at stages 15–16 were observed, as shown in Figure 1F and G, respectively, with 100% penetrance (stage 12: eight embryos, stage 15–16: ten embryos).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of the phenotype across multiple embryos.

claim: Overexpression of trh by R14E10-GAL4 in trh mutants rescued the phenotype.
source: In addition, the overexpression of trh (trh-OE) by R14E10-GAL4 in the trh mutants rescued the phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: breathless encodes an FGF receptor.
source: One of the Trh target genes is breathless (btl), which encodes an FGF receptor (Ohshiro and Saigo, 1997), and we reported that FGF signaling through Btl is able to trigger invagination independent of EGF signaling and mitotic rounding (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: FGF signaling through Btl is able to trigger invagination independent of EGF signaling and mitotic rounding.
source: One of the Trh target genes is breathless (btl), which encodes an FGF receptor (Ohshiro and Saigo, 1997), and we reported that FGF signaling through Btl is able to trigger invagination independent of EGF signaling and mitotic rounding (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: btl overexpression in trh mutants using R14E10-GAL4 did not rescue tracheal formation from the transiently invaginated tracheal placodes.
source: However, the btl-OE in the trh mutants using R14E10-GAL4 did not rescue tracheal formation from the transiently invaginated tracheal placodes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), indicating that other trh target genes are required to support FGF signaling-triggered tracheal morphogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Other trh target genes are required to support FGF signaling-triggered tracheal morphogenesis.
source: However, the btl-OE in the trh mutants using R14E10-GAL4 did not rescue tracheal formation from the transiently invaginated tracheal placodes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), indicating that other trh target genes are required to support FGF signaling-triggered tracheal morphogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the failure of btl overexpression to rescue the trh mutant phenotype.

claim: Inhibiting apoptosis by p35 did not prevent the transiently invaginated cells from returning to the epidermis.
source: In addition, inhibiting apoptosis by p35 did not prevent the transiently invaginated cells from returning to the epidermis, indicating that apoptotic cell removal is not the major cause of this anomaly (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Apoptotic cell removal is not the major cause of transiently invaginated cells returning to the epidermis in trh mutants.
source: In addition, inhibiting apoptosis by p35 did not prevent the transiently invaginated cells from returning to the epidermis, indicating that apoptotic cell removal is not the major cause of this anomaly (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the p35 overexpression experiment.

claim: Tracheal formation proceeds by two successive and genetically separable steps: (1) invagination triggered by mechanical forces and (2) maintenance of the invaginated structure controlled by trh.
source: These results demonstrated that trh is essential for maintaining the invaginated structure, whereas it is dispensable for initiating invagination. Thus, tracheal formation proceeds by two successive and genetically separable steps: (1) invagination triggered by the mechanical forces generated through the combined activities of mitosis, EGFR, and FGFR signaling; and (2) maintenance of the invaginated structure controlled by trh.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing trh is dispensable for initiation but essential for maintenance.

claim: Mitosis-triggered invagination was maintained in rho bnl mutants.
source: Since mitosis-triggered invagination was maintained in rho bnl mutants (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013), EGFR and FGFR signaling are dispensable for the maintenance of the invaginated structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EGFR and FGFR signaling are dispensable for the maintenance of the invaginated structure.
source: Since mitosis-triggered invagination was maintained in rho bnl mutants (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013), EGFR and FGFR signaling are dispensable for the maintenance of the invaginated structure.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mitosis-triggered invagination is maintained in rho bnl mutants.

claim: JAK-STAT signaling induces trh expression through a STAT-responsive trh enhancer in the tracheal placodes at stage 10 of embryogenesis before invagination.
source: JAK-STAT signaling induces trh expression through a STAT-responsive trh enhancer in the tracheal placodes at stage 10 of embryogenesis before invagination (Figure 2A) (Brown et al., 2001; Sotillos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: After invagination, Trh is detected only in all invaginated cells, including the most proximal spiracular branch.
source: After invagination, Trh is detected only in all invaginated cells, including the most proximal spiracular branch (Figure 2C,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C,F.

claim: The number of initial Trh+ cells in the tracheal placode before invagination (stage 10) was 58.2 ± 5.1 (mean ±S.D.) in controls and 67.2 ± 8.5 in the rho bnl mutants.
source: The number of initial Trh+ cells in the tracheal placode before invagination (stage 10) was 58.2 ± 5.1 (mean ±S.D.) in controls and 67.2 ± 8.5 in the rho bnl mutants, respectively, indicating that tracheal fate specification was not compromised in the rho bnl mutants (Figure 2A,B,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Tracheal fate specification was not compromised in the rho bnl mutants.
source: The number of initial Trh+ cells in the tracheal placode before invagination (stage 10) was 58.2 ± 5.1 (mean ±S.D.) in controls and 67.2 ± 8.5 in the rho bnl mutants, respectively, indicating that tracheal fate specification was not compromised in the rho bnl mutants (Figure 2A,B,G).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar number of initial Trh+ cells in control and rho bnl mutants.

claim: The increase in the number of initial Trh+ cells in the rho bnl placodes reflects the expansion of the tracheal placode due to the earlier role of rho in restricting the size of tracheal placode.
source: The increase in the number of initial Trh+ cells in the rho bnl placodes reflects the expansion of the tracheal placode due to the earlier role of rho in restricting the size of tracheal placode (Raz and Shilo, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The number of initial R14E10 + cells (57.9 ± 2.7 cells, monitored by using the R14E10-lacZ transgene at stage 10) is almost the same as the number of initial Trh+ cells.
source: The R14E10 fragment contains the trh66 STAT-responsive element that mediates stage9-10 trh expression (Sotillos et al., 2010), and the number of initial R14E10 + cells (57.9 ± 2.7 cells, monitored by using the R14E10-lacZ transgene at stage 10) is almost the same as the number of initial Trh+ cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data.

claim: After cycle-16 mitosis and invagination, the resultant tracheae of the rho bnl mutants were composed of a smaller number of Trh+ cells (trh-on cells, 31.2 ± 6.2 cells) than those of the controls (87.6 ± 6.3 cells).
source: In contrast, after cycle-16 mitosis and invagination, the resultant tracheae of the rho bnl mutants were composed of a smaller number of Trh+ cells (trh-on cells, 31.2 ± 6.2 cells) than those of the controls (87.6 ± 6.3 cells) (Figure 2C,D,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In the rho bnl mutants, the number of initial Trh+ cells at stage 10 was reduced at stages 13–14.
source: These findings demonstrate that in the rho bnl mutants, the number of initial Trh+ cells at stage 10 was reduced at stages 13–14.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of initial Trh+ cells and later trh-on cells in rho bnl mutants.

claim: The reduction in Trh+ cells in rho bnl mutants is due to either the disappearance of Trh+ cells from the epithelium or the loss of Trh expression in cells that failed to invaginate.
source: This reduction is due to either the disappearance of Trh+ cells from the epithelium or the loss of Trh expression in cells that failed to invaginate.
evidence: This is a logical inference about possible mechanisms for the observed reduction.

claim: The R14E10-GAL4-induced nls-lacZ product (β-galactosidase, β-gal) persisted in the initial trh+ cells after termination of R14E10-GAL4 transcription.
source: The R14E10-GAL4-induced nls-lacZ product (β-galactosidase, β-gal) persisted in the initial trh+ cells after termination of R14E10-GAL4 transcription, allowing us to distinguish trh-off (Trh–, LacZ+) and trh-on (Trh+) cells derived from the initial trh-on cell population after invagination (from stage 13 onward).
evidence: This describes the experimental strategy for lineage tracing.

claim: In control embryos, there were trh-off cells (31.9 ± 6.7 cells) in the epidermis.
source: Even in control embryos, there were trh-off cells (31.9 ± 6.7 cells) in the epidermis (Figure 2C,G), while all of the trh-on cells were found in the invaginated tubule region (87.6 ± 6.3 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In control embryos, all of the trh-on cells were found in the invaginated tubule region (87.6 ± 6.3 cells).
source: Even in control embryos, there were trh-off cells (31.9 ± 6.7 cells) in the epidermis (Figure 2C,G), while all of the trh-on cells were found in the invaginated tubule region (87.6 ± 6.3 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The sum of the trh-on and trh-off cells (119.5 ± 10.5 cells) agreed well with the prediction from the number of initial Trh+ cells (58.2 ± 5.1 cells) and the number of initial R14E10 + cells (57.9 ± 2.7 cells) after one round of cycle-16 mitosis during invagination.
source: The sum of the trh-on and trh-off cells (119.5 ± 10.5 cells) agreed well with the prediction from the number of initial Trh+ cells (58.2 ± 5.1 cells) and the number of initial R14E10 + cells (57.9 ± 2.7 cells, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C) after one round of cycle-16 mitosis during invagination.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cell numbers.

claim: 27% of the initial trh+ cells lost their Trh expression, all of which remained in the epidermis.
source: The results showed that 27% of the initial trh+ cells lost their Trh expression, all of which remained in the epidermis.
evidence: This claim is calculated from the quantitative cell counting data.

claim: Many of the trh-off cells remained during the rest of embryogenesis and formed trichomes on their apical surface.
source: Many of the trh-off cells remained during the rest of embryogenesis and formed trichomes on their apical surface (data not shown), suggesting that they adopted the epidermal fate.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of trichome formation.

claim: trh-off cells adopted the epidermal fate.
source: Many of the trh-off cells remained during the rest of embryogenesis and formed trichomes on their apical surface (data not shown), suggesting that they adopted the epidermal fate.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that trh-off cells form trichomes, a characteristic of epidermal cells.

claim: In rho bnl mutants after invagination, the resultant tracheae were composed of 31.2 ± 6.2 trh-on cells and surrounded by 50.4 ± 7.2 epidermal trh-off cells, with a total of 81.6 ± 9.8 cells.
source: After invagination, the resultant tracheae were composed of a smaller number of trh-on cells (31.2 ± 6.2 cells), as mentioned above, and surrounded by an increased number of epidermal trh-off cells (50.4 ± 7.2 cells) than those of the controls, with a total of 81.6 ± 9.8 cells (Figure 2D,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Blocking apoptosis by p35 in the rho bnl mutants increased the number of both trh-on and trh-off cells.
source: Blocking apoptosis by p35 in the rho bnl mutants increased the number of both trh-on and trh-off cells (Figure 2E,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In the rho bnl mutants with or without p35, 62% of the surviving initial trh+ cells remained in the epidermis and lost their trh expression.
source: In the rho bnl mutants with or without p35, 62% of the surviving initial trh+ cells remained in the epidermis and lost their trh expression.
evidence: This claim is calculated from the quantitative cell counting data.

claim: The reduction in trh-on cells in the rho bnl mutants was not simply due to their disappearance from the epithelium.
source: These findings indicated that the reduction in trh-on cells in the rho bnl mutants was not simply due to their disappearance from the epithelium.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that blocking apoptosis increases both trh-on and trh-off cells.

claim: Losses of EGF, FGF, and mitosis in the rho CyclinA (CycA) bnl triple mutant caused a more severe invagination defect.
source: Losses of EGF, FGF, and mitosis in the rho CyclinA (CycA) bnl triple mutant caused a more severe invagination defect (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The initial trh expression at stage 10 was nearly normal even in the rho CycA bnl triple mutant (53.9 ± 7.1 cells).
source: The initial trh expression at stage 10 was nearly normal even in the triple mutant (53.9 ± 7.1 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The number of Trh-on tracheal cells in rho CycA bnl triple mutants was 6.0 ± 2.5 cells.
source: However, although all the invaginated cells were Trh-positive, the number of Trh-on tracheal cells in these triple mutants was much smaller than expected (6.0 ± 2.5 cells, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), which strongly argues against the model in which the tube-forming trh-on cells are predetermined before invagination.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The observation that the number of Trh-on cells in rho CycA bnl triple mutants is much smaller than expected strongly argues against the model in which the tube-forming trh-on cells are predetermined before invagination.
source: However, although all the invaginated cells were Trh-positive, the number of Trh-on tracheal cells in these triple mutants was much smaller than expected (6.0 ± 2.5 cells, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), which strongly argues against the model in which the tube-forming trh-on cells are predetermined before invagination.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the quantitative data.

claim: The trh expression in the stage 10 tracheal placodes is maintained only in the successfully invaginated tubule cells, independent of the depth of invagination.
source: These observations support the possibility that the trh expression in the stage 10 tracheal placodes is maintained only in the successfully invaginated tubule cells, independent of the depth of invagination.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observations in various mutants.

claim: The placode cells that failed to invaginate and remained in the epidermis lost their trh expression.
source: The placode cells that failed to invaginate and remained in the epidermis lost their trh expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing experiments showing trh-off cells in the epidermis.

claim: A mechanism exists to maintain trh expression only in the invaginated tubule cells and extinguish it in the superficial epidermal cells.
source: These results imply that a mechanism exists to maintain trh expression only in the invaginated tubule cells and extinguish it in the superficial epidermal cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observations of differential trh expression in invaginated vs. epidermal cells.

claim: A transcriptional reporter of trh [1-eve-1, a lacZ enhancer trap of trh] elicited reporter β-gal expression that was limited to the invaginated tracheal cells.
source: A transcriptional reporter of trh [1-eve-1, a lacZ enhancer trap of trh (Perrimon et al., 1991; Wilk et al., 1996) elicited reporter β-gal expression that was limited to the invaginated tracheal cells (Figure 3B), suggesting that the epidermal expression of trh is repressed at the level of transcription.
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The epidermal expression of trh is repressed at the level of transcription.
source: A transcriptional reporter of trh [1-eve-1, a lacZ enhancer trap of trh (Perrimon et al., 1991; Wilk et al., 1996) elicited reporter β-gal expression that was limited to the invaginated tracheal cells (Figure 3B), suggesting that the epidermal expression of trh is repressed at the level of transcription.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that a transcriptional reporter is limited to tracheal cells.

claim: trh47 and trh66 are primary enhancers that drive reporter expression from the early stage of tracheal development.
source: Among the eight trh upstream regions with phylogenetically conserved STAT-binding sites, trh47 and trh66 drive reporter expression from the early stage of tracheal development, and trh67 is proposed to be a trh-dependent auto-regulatory element (Sotillos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: trh67 is proposed to be a trh-dependent auto-regulatory element.
source: Among the eight trh upstream regions with phylogenetically conserved STAT-binding sites, trh47 and trh66 drive reporter expression from the early stage of tracheal development, and trh67 is proposed to be a trh-dependent auto-regulatory element (Sotillos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The two primary enhancers, trh47 and trh66, were active in both tubule cells and the surrounding epidermal cells.
source: We found that the two primary enhancers, trh47 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and trh66 (covered by R14E10, Figure 3A, Figures 1D and 2C), were active in both tubule cells and the surrounding epidermal cells, suggesting that they did not reproduce the epidermal extinction of trh.
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and other figures.

claim: trh47 and trh66 did not reproduce the epidermal extinction of trh.
source: We found that the two primary enhancers, trh47 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and trh66 (covered by R14E10, Figure 3A, Figures 1D and 2C), were active in both tubule cells and the surrounding epidermal cells, suggesting that they did not reproduce the epidermal extinction of trh.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that these enhancers are active in both tracheal and epidermal cells.

claim: trh67 did not drive reporter expression in all of the Trh-positive invaginated cells.
source: In contrast, trh67 did not drive reporter expression in all of the Trh-positive invaginated cells, suggesting that additional cis-elements control the tube-specific maintenance of trh expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Additional cis-elements control the tube-specific maintenance of trh expression.
source: In contrast, trh67 did not drive reporter expression in all of the Trh-positive invaginated cells, suggesting that additional cis-elements control the tube-specific maintenance of trh expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the incomplete expression pattern of trh67.

claim: R15F01 showed strict tube-specific activity after invagination, and its activity was maintained in the invaginated tubule cells throughout embryogenesis.
source: R15F01 showed strict tube-specific activity after invagination, and its activity was maintained in the invaginated tubule cells throughout embryogenesis (Figure 3B', G) and in postembryonic stages (not shown), in contrast to trh47 and trh66 (R14E10), which show transient activity only from embryonic stage 10 to 11 (Sotillos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3B', G.

claim: trh47 and trh66 (R14E10) show transient activity only from embryonic stage 10 to 11.
source: R15F01 showed strict tube-specific activity after invagination, and its activity was maintained in the invaginated tubule cells throughout embryogenesis (Figure 3B', G) and in postembryonic stages (not shown), in contrast to trh47 and trh66 (R14E10), which show transient activity only from embryonic stage 10 to 11 (Sotillos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A few epidermal cells sporadically showed leaked R15F01 activity, especially when monitored using R15F01-GAL4 reporter transgenes.
source: We note that a few epidermal cells sporadically showed leaked R15F01 activity, especially when we monitored the activity using R15F01-GAL4 reporter transgenes (Figure 3B').
evidence: This claim is based on observation of reporter expression.

claim: When using a direct lacZ reporter (R15F01-lacZ), R15F01's activity became detectable in part of the tracheal placode before invagination.
source: In addition, when we used a direct lacZ reporter (R15F01-lacZ), R15F01's activity became detectable in part of the tracheal placode before invagination (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2G), slightly later than that of the other early enhancers (trh47 or R14E10).
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: R15F01 repressed the function of an adjacent mini-yellow gene in the adult epidermis.
source: In addition, we noticed that R15F01 repressed the function of an adjacent mini-yellow gene (mini-y included in attP40 or attP2, a transgene landing site on chromosome 2L or chromosome 3L, respectively [Groth et al., 2004]) in the adult epidermis (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of adult fly body color shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The function of the endogenous yellow gene on chromosome X was not affected by R15F01.
source: The function of the endogenous yellow gene on chromosome X was not affected (data not shown), suggesting that R15F01 represses mini-y expression in cis.
evidence: This claim is based on observation.

claim: R15F01 represses mini-y expression in cis.
source: The function of the endogenous yellow gene on chromosome X was not affected (data not shown), suggesting that R15F01 represses mini-y expression in cis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that endogenous yellow is not affected while mini-y is repressed.

claim: R15F01 is a cis-regulatory module (CRM) that simultaneously functions as an enhancer in tracheal tube cells and a silencer in epidermal sheet cells.
source: These results suggested that R15F01 is a cis-regulatory module (CRM) that simultaneously functions as an enhancer in tracheal tube cells and a silencer in epidermal sheet cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the dual activity of R15F01 in different cell types.

claim: In mutant combinations that prevented invagination to various degrees, no or only a few epidermal cells showed R15F01 activity, while the small tracheal tubes were R15F01-positive irrespective of the depth of invagination.
source: Using the mutant combinations that prevented invagination to various degrees (combinations of rho, bnl and CycA), no or only a few epidermal cells showed R15F01 activity, while the small tracheal tubes were R15F01-positive irrespective of the depth of invagination (Figure 3C,D,H–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data in various mutants shown in Figure 3C,D,H–K.

claim: In the rho bnl mutants, R15F01 activation was detected at stage 10 before invagination.
source: In the rho bnl mutants, R15F01 activation was detected at stage 10 before invagination.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of reporter expression.

claim: The number of initial R15F01 + cells in the rho bnl mutants before cycle-16 mitosis and invagination (39.5 ± 4.7 cells) is smaller than that of control embryos (47.3 ± 6.1).

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.
